concerns: Assay-interference risk: formulation excipients or mucin components can mask epitopes or inhibit capture reagents leading to false-negative ‘‘loss’’ unless capture-compatibility panels and buffer prequalification are comprehensive (MISEV2023 warns about separation/characterization artifacts).

Spike-in representativeness: an orthogonal exogenous tracer may not recapitulate endogenous EV surface chemistry, leading to misleading recovery validation; multiple spike-ins or differently labeled orthogonal tracers would strengthen inference.

Non-vesicular activity: preserved anti-inflammatory signal after passage could derive from soluble proteins or mucin-bound factors (rodent intranasal efficacy studies show bioactivity but did not prove membrane protection). Protease ± detergent controls mitigate this but may not fully exclude protected non-vesicular complexes (e.g., lipoproteins, protein–mucin aggregates) without additional orthogonal separation/identification (e.g., density, proteomics).

Species/administration generalizability: macaque intranasal biodistribution was poor despite intranasal dosing—an in vitro compatibility pass may not predict in vivo delivery or detectability in larger species; program should avoid overinterpreting an in vitro ‘‘pass’’ as sufficient for clinical translation.

Low biomass and assay sensitivity: captured eluates may contain very low particle/protein mass; cell-based cytokine assays may lack sensitivity or be variably affected by residual excipients, requiring rigorous LOD/controls and possibly signal amplification strategies.

Detergent/protease specificity: loss of signal after detergent/protease is consistent with membrane protection but is not uniquely diagnostic—some non-vesicular complexes may also be susceptible or resistant depending on composition; combine with orthogonal markers (multiple tetraspanins, phospholipid stains, lipidomic signatures).
conclusion: The proposed spike-in–controlled mucin + device-shear compatibility experiment is a plausible, well-rationalized in vitro gate that addresses key risks called out by MISEV2023 and leverages prior rodent intranasal bioactivity reports. It is likely to discriminate at least two major competing explanations (assay interference vs true membrane damage; vesicle-associated vs non-vesicular soluble activity) when the specified spike-in, detergent/protease protection, capture co-localization, and protected-bioactivity readouts are implemented and validated. However, important evidence gaps remain (notably large-animal in vivo relevance, representativeness of mucin mimics and device shear, and low-biomass bioassay sensitivity), and several additional orthogonal controls and assay validations will be needed to reduce false positives/negatives before using the gate to advance formulations toward in vivo bridging.
evidence_gap: Key gaps: (1) translational relevance to larger species—macaque data show poor intranasal biodistribution so an in vivo bridging strategy (or additional large-animal biodistribution experiments) is needed to link an in vitro ‘‘pass’’ to meaningful exposure; (2) validation that the selected mucin-mimic and device-shear rig faithfully reproduce clinically relevant stresses (dose, residence time, shear profiles); (3) confirmation that the exogenous spike-in tracer behaves like the endogenous EV population across the tested formulation/device matrix (biophysical and capture-epitope similarity); (4) demonstration that the low-biomass captured eluates provide robust, reproducible cytokine readouts (assay LOD/LOQ and lot-to-lot variability).
